label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
Nana,

Denise is reading this to you because I'm stuck in Toronto, which you already know, and which I've already apologized for about six times on the phone. So I'll keep that part short. I'm sorry I'm not sitting at that table with you tonight. I wanted to be. I tried to get someone to cover for me and couldn't, and I've felt lousy about it all week. Everybody keeps telling me it's fine and that you understand, and I know you do. I still wish I was there. That's all I'll say about it.

(Denise, if she's already reaching for a Kleenex, tell her to hang on, it gets better.)

I've been trying to write this for over a week, and every time I started I'd get about two lines in and have to close the laptop. That house does that to me. So I'm going to try to tell you what it meant to me without making it sound like a funeral, because it isn't one. You're moving to a place with a crib league. That's not sad. That's a promotion.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. I've been doing the math on that and it doesn't really fit in my head. That kitchen you're sitting in right now has had more of this family in it than any other room on earth. You raised half of us in there, fed the other half, and sent everybody home with leftovers whether they wanted them or not. When I think about the house, I mostly think about that kitchen, and when I think about that kitchen I mostly think about you. I'm not sure there's a difference.

I think about the summers a lot. Every year I'd show up thinking I was getting a vacation, and every year I found out I was actually getting a job. If I dried the dishes, I could stay up and watch the Expos, and later the Jays, on that little TV in the kitchen. I'd like to say I dried them because I was a good kid, but I think we both know I was doing it for the baseball. You knew that too, and you let me do it anyway. Some of the best nights of my life were standing at that counter with a wet dish towel, watching a game on a screen the size of a cereal box, and you telling me I'd missed a spot.

And then crib. You taught me when I was about seven and you never once let me win. Not once. Other kids had grandmothers who'd go easy on them. Mine counted my hand for me and then took the points I'd missed. I lost to you for eight straight years. I'm not exaggerating, I've done the math on that one too. Then I was fifteen, and I finally skunked you, and I was so proud of myself I could barely sit still. And instead of being annoyed, you got up and made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still think that's the best thing anyone's ever done for me. It taught me that you actually earn things, and that when you do, somebody who loves you will notice. I've carried that around my whole life. I also still think about those tarts more than is probably normal.

I think about the back steps too. You'd be out there at six in the morning with your tea, and if I wandered out half asleep, I learned fast that you weren't talking until that cup was empty. So I'd just sit beside you and we'd look at the yard and not say anything. I didn't appreciate it then, but those are some of my favourite memories of you. Not every good minute needs talking in it. I didn't know that until I sat on those steps.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." I still have that card. I didn't spend the twenty. Actually, that's a lie, I spent it on pizza, because you told me to and I wasn't about to argue. But I kept the card. It's on my fridge.

And I have to say, I love that every time I call now, you ask me if anything broke. Ever since my pager went off at Christmas dinner and you asked if the internet was broken again and whether I'd fixed it. For the record, Nana, the internet was not broken. One very small piece of it was having a bad night. But I like your version better, so from now on it's the official one. Yes, I fix the internet. You can tell the church ladies. You probably already have.

Here's the thing I really wanted to say, and I want Denise to read this part slowly so you actually hear it.

I'm proud of you.

You picked this. Nobody made you. Nobody sat you down and told you it was time. You looked at it yourself, you went and saw the place, you decided, and you did it. I know people your age who'd hang on to their house until somebody had to drag them out of it, and I know how hard it must be to leave a place you've been in for fifty-one years. You're doing it on your own terms, with your head up, and kind of excited about it. That takes more guts than most people have at any age. I hope I'm half that sensible when I'm eighty-eight. Odds aren't great, but I hope.

And honestly, Elmwood looks nice. I looked it all up, I'm not going to pretend I didn't. Second floor, a window that looks out on the parking lot and a big maple. I know the parking lot part isn't very romantic, but you'll get to see who's coming and going and keep track of everybody, which, let's be honest, you'd be doing anyway. And the maple's going to look great in the fall. You'll have your Tuesday crib with the church ladies, and now there's a whole league on top of that. I feel bad for those people. They have no idea what's coming. I give it a month before you're running the thing.

I don't think the house really stays behind, either. I know that sounds like something off a sympathy card, but I mean it. Everything good that happened in that kitchen happened because you were in it. The house was just where we kept you. Now we'll keep you at Elmwood, and we'll all just have to learn a new route and a new parking spot.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I asked for the crib board, which I'm sure surprises nobody. I want you to know it's not because I want something to remember the house by. It's because I want to keep playing on it. With you.

So here's the plan. I'm coming up the weekend of December 5th, as soon as my rotation's done. I'm bringing the crib board, and we're playing the first game at the new place, by that window with the maple. I've been practicing. I'm not going to tell you how much. I fully expect you not to let me win, and I wouldn't want you to. If I somehow skunk you again, I'll accept payment in butter tarts, but I'll understand if your new kitchen isn't set up yet. I can wait.

Until then, settle in, boss those people around a bit, and save me a seat by the window.

And no, Nana, nothing broke this week. Except me, a couple of times, trying to write this.

I love you. See you on the 5th.

[your name]

---

It comes to about 1,350 words, so roughly eight or nine minutes read aloud at an easy pace. You might want to give Denise a copy ahead of time so she's not reading it cold. The bracketed line to her near the start is optional. Some families find that kind of aside funny when it's read aloud, but cut it if it feels off. The main laughs are the eight-year losing streak, "for the record, the internet was not broken," and the crib league line. If anything doesn't sound like how you'd actually say it to her, tell me and I'll adjust it.
